summary: American filibuster William Walker invaded Mexico's Baja California in 1853, then seized Nicaragua in 1855-1857, declaring himself president, legalising slavery and burning Granada, before Honduras executed him in 1860.

evidence.note: birth in Nashville, Tennessee in 1824 and slaveholding family background
buys into the Daily Crescent; later edits papers in San Francisco and Sacramento
long segment on Narciso Lopez's filibuster plans for Cuba, backed in Walker's editorials
1853 scouting trip to Guaymas, first step toward the Sonora invasion
takes La Paz by force and proclaims the Republic of Lower California with himself president
adopts Louisiana law for his Mexican republic, making slavery legal by default
rancher Melendrez raises militias that besiege Ensenada and retake San Vicente
invited into the Nicaraguan civil war, sails 1855 and takes Granada
1856 decree reinstating slavery in Nicaragua and his racial plans for the country
Costa Rica declares war; fighting at Santa Rosa and Rivas
Roatan venture, British hand him to Honduras, execution in 1860
closing segment on his memory in Central America and a modern libertarian review

notes: Transcript gives the San Francisco indictment as 1864; historically 1854, which fits the sequence. Meléndrez dates unknown, floruit 1853-54. dictator-autocrat reflects his self-installed presidency of Nicaragua; colonial-administrator was the alternative. reaches_present rests on a ~4 minute closing segment on legacy and a Cato review; borderline. hate-speech for repeated quotation of his racist writings.
